paragraphs.heading: What is changing
paragraphs.text: Climate change is affecting both Earth's natural environment and human societies, and the effects are well documented and growing. Global warming touches every part of Earth's climate system. The changes include an overall warming trend, shifts in precipitation patterns and more extreme weather. The rise in global surface temperatures so far is 1.1 °C (2.0 °F), and scientists say they will rise further in the future.

paragraphs.heading: Warming is uneven
paragraphs.text: The effects differ in timing and location, and the climate is not changing in a uniform way across the Earth. Most areas of land have warmed faster than most areas of ocean. Air temperatures at the surface over land have risen at about twice the ocean rate, causing intense heat waves. Climate change feedbacks have so far made the Arctic warm faster than most other regions. Nights have also warmed faster than days.

paragraphs.heading: Oceans and ice respond slowly
paragraphs.text: If greenhouse gas emissions were brought under control, surface temperatures would stabilize. But ice sheets and oceans absorb the vast majority of the excess heat in the atmosphere. This delays the effects there, yet causes them to speed up and then carry on after surface temperatures have stabilized. As a result, sea level rise is a particular concern over the long term. A warming ocean also brings marine heatwaves and changes to ocean currents, and the ocean is acidifying as it takes in carbon dioxide from the atmosphere.

paragraphs.heading: Pressure on living things
paragraphs.text: The ecosystems most immediately threatened are in the mountains, coral reefs and the Arctic. Excess heat is changing the environment in those places beyond what animals are able to adapt to. Where they can, species are escaping the heat by moving towards the poles and to higher ground. Rising seas threaten coastal wetlands with flooding. In certain locations, a drop in soil moisture can cause desertification and harm ecosystems such as the Amazon rainforest. With 2 °C (3.6 °F) of warming, about 10% of land species would become critically endangered.

paragraphs.heading: Effects on people
paragraphs.text: Humans are vulnerable in many ways. Environmental changes can threaten sources of food and fresh water. Health can be affected by weather extremes or by ripple effects such as the spread of infectious diseases. Economic impacts include changes to farming, fisheries and forestry, and in tropical latitudes heat stress will increasingly prevent outdoor work. Rising seas may inundate island nations and coastal cities, and extreme weather events and cumulative effects can lead to displacement and migration.

paragraphs.heading: Who is most at risk
paragraphs.text: Some groups of people may be particularly at risk, such as the poor, children and indigenous peoples. Countries differ as well. Industrialised countries have emitted the vast majority of CO₂, and they have more resources than developing nations for adapting to global warming.

paragraphs.heading: Clues from the past
paragraphs.text: One way scientists predict the effects of human-caused climate change is to investigate natural climate changes in the past. To do this they have studied tree rings, ice cores, corals and the sediments of oceans and lakes. These show that recent temperatures have gone beyond anything in the last 2,000 years. By the end of the 21st century, temperatures may reach a level last seen in the mid-Pliocene, around 3 million years ago. Back then, mean global temperatures stood about 2–4 °C (3.6–7.2 °F) above pre-industrial temperatures, and the global mean sea level reached as much as 25 metres (82 ft) above today's.
